question: Why should we care whether another group is within the fold of Islam, and how should we treat other sects?
asked: I am Sunni, but I am very distressed at seeing other groups always declared kafir, and the sectarian bias in our country is destroying our society. Why can't we just let people claim that they're Muslims and let Allah judge? What can be done about sectarianism, and why should we even care whether another group is within or outside the fold of Islam?
answer:
This question is actually very pertinent. It's actually very difficult. It's also very necessary. This is a very important chapter in all of our books of theology, and I'm going to try to summarize some important aspects that we need to be aware of, with of course the understanding that this is a much more detailed topic. And in fact it is one of the branches of theology, one of the branches of the science of aqeedah: who gets to declare, and how is that declaration made, and why is that declaration made, about which theology expels one from Islam or not.

So I'm going to start off by stating that, firstly, she asked from a very specific nation state, and I'm going to answer theoretically. I'm not going to get involved with that particular nation state. I'm going to talk theoretically about the issue of why we care. What are we worried about? Why do we say this group is right and wrong, or this group is outside the fold of Islam? Why can't we just self-identify? That's the question she's asking: if somebody says they're Muslim, why do we have to get involved and say, hold on a sec, your belief here is right or wrong?

So I'm not going to mention specifically about that one country. And then towards the end of my remarks, inshallah, we'll talk a little bit more about the practical realities that might be culture-specific. Because the question has two paradigms to look at it from: the theoretical, which is independent of where you are in the world, and then the practical, which might change from time to time and from place to place. And I'm more interested in the theoretical, and then I'll give some remarks about the practical.

Now the issue of who is or isn't a Muslim has concerned every single group of Islam since the beginning of Islam, and it should be of concern to all of us. We should be very concerned, because Islam is our way of salvation. And just like we are concerned with what it means to be a good human being, what it means to be a good citizen, how we can be better people, we should be even more concerned about how we can be better Muslims. And we will not know what it means to be a good Muslim unless and until we also know what it means to be the opposite. We will not know the reality of iman unless we also study the reality of the opposite of iman.

Because one understands things by the opposites, right? One understands things by looking at the good and looking at the bad. So you know what is the importance of being healthy, for example. Now you study what happens when you're not healthy. You study what happens when you smoke cigarettes and what happens to your lungs, right? You study what happens when your cholesterol level is high, and you get an awareness that is different than the awareness of the positives of being healthy. Put together, knowing the positives of being healthy and the negatives of being unhealthy, you automatically develop an awareness to live a better lifestyle. You need to know the positives and you also need to know the negatives.

And this is in the Qur'an. Allah says in the Qur'an, "And this is how We clarify the signs, so that the paths of those who are criminals," or those that are wrong, "can be made clear to you." The paths of those that are doing wrong should be made clear to you. And also the famous hadith as well of Hudhayfa radiyallahu 'anhu, that he said: the people used to ask the Prophet ﷺ about good things, but I would ask him about the problems and the fitnas and the trials. I would ask about the evil things because I wanted to avoid falling into them.

So a part of our religion is to know what is bad religion. And therefore we should be concerned about definitions. What does it mean to be a Muslim? What does it mean to be a good Muslim? Hence, what does it mean to be a bad Muslim?

As well, the concept of defining what is Islam: actually, every word needs to be defined. There's no question about it. Think about it. You need to define every single term, whether you're talking about a term in a scientific discipline or a term in a political discourse. When you use a term, that term has to have a definition. And that's why legal contracts are so difficult for us to understand, because they have to define each and every term in that contract. But that's what happens when you use important terms. Which term is more important than the term Islam? Isn't it the most important term? And therefore, when you're using the term Islam, by definition, when you say Islam, you must mean something. When you mean something, you're excluding other things as well.

So this notion of "why should we care", we should reverse it around and say there should be nothing we should be more concerned with than to know what is good faith and good iman, so that we can apply it. Now, us applying it is different than, obviously, treating other people, which we're going to come to. My point right now is this notion of why should we care? No, we should care because it makes us better people. We should care because we should have a relationship with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, which is the best relationship. So we need to know what is iman and what is the opposite of iman.

And we need to understand as well that we are not obliged by Allah to pass verdicts about inner intentions or about heaven and hell. But we can and we should pass verdicts on actions. You see, again, we have to have that fine distinction here. What we are seeing now in the modern culture is this notion of "Who are we to judge? Don't judge me," right? And this is a statement that has some correct and some incorrect meanings.

Every society judges people based upon their outer actions. Every society. You're going to go to jail because of certain actions that you did, right? You're not going to get away. The thief or the criminal cannot come to the court and say, "Don't judge me." The murderer cannot come and say, "Don't judge me." We will judge every single person based upon what they have done. So then why should iman be any different? Why should orthodoxy be any different? We judge people based upon the outer, but we do not judge intentions. And most importantly, we do not judge the hereafter.

This is a very key point that sometimes even preachers and teachers mix up. If I say something is wrong Islamically, I am judging the action. I am not judging the person doing the action and pronouncing a verdict that that person is going to heaven or hell. That's the difference here. I can and I will say drinking alcohol is wrong. If I were to meet an alcoholic, somebody addicted to alcohol, that is a separate issue, and I'm not judging this person's heaven and hell. I'm not judging whether Allah is going to be merciful or not. On the contrary, that is a totally distinct aspect that has nothing to do with saying drinking alcohol is wrong.

Am I not allowed to say that alcoholic drinks are haram and sinful? And then if I meet an alcoholic, he's going to come and say, "Oh, don't judge me." I'm still going to tell him drinking alcoholic drinks is haram, but I ask him that, you know, we are all sinners; turn to Allah in repentance; Allah forgives sins. So we distinguish between theoretically talking about an action and judging a person. We judge the action of the person, and as for the person himself or herself, we leave their affair to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And this applies to the Muslim and to the kafir. We do not pronounce verdicts of the hereafter on any individual. That doesn't change the fact that we shall pronounce verdicts on actions and on beliefs in this world, and we shall treat people based upon their outer deeds.

If you know somebody is a convicted murderer, are you not going to be acting differently around that person? It's the reality of life. If you know somebody is a very dangerous person, you're going to take your own precautions. You're not judging their hereafter, but there is a certain methodology with which you will interact with that person.

So we have to be, again, careful of the middle line, the middle balance here, between understanding that we are obliged by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to speak generically about good deeds and bad deeds (we invite people to good deeds and we warn people from bad deeds; we invite people to good theology, we warn people against bad theology) versus the individual that has good and bad, that we might treat nicely or we might treat harshly. We might treat them with sympathy; we might treat them with a little bit of harshness.

A simple example is if a relative of yours is a drug dealer, right? You want to get the message across: I don't like what you're doing; I'm not going to be satisfied. A cousin of yours is a drug dealer, is in the local mafia. I'm just giving a very far-fetched example. I hope it's far-fetched, inshallah. But suppose you have a cousin that's in the drug mafia, the drug cartel. Can you just ignore the fact that he's doing something that is harmful to himself, to his family, to his society? You're not going to ignore that. Even if you meet him outside of his cartel activities or his haram activities, you visit him and whatnot, even as you meet him there will be this awareness in you and in him that there is something that is not 100% right.

So all of this needs to be taken into account, and it's not an easy topic to summarize in, you know, 15–20 minutes. Nonetheless, I'll try to give you some generic guidelines. Okay, that was all an introduction, by the way.

The first point that I wanted to mention is that the issue of who is and who isn't a Muslim is something, as I already mentioned in the introduction, that is of crucial importance. And in fact, one can say the companions themselves showed us how important this is at the death of the Prophet, when the wars of the apostasy took place, what is called the Hurub al-Ridda. When they took place, the companions themselves began discussing this issue: are these people within or outside the fold of Islam? And they had to treat them differently.

Certain groups claimed that there were prophets after the Prophet ﷺ, most prominently Musaylama and Sajjah, and they were considered to be outside the fold of Islam. Other groups said they're not going to pay zakat. And Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, now here there's a controversy: did he view them as being apostates, or did he view them as being rebels? And Allah knows best, but it appears that those people who denied the obligation to pay zakat, he viewed them as being non-Muslims. And those that were greedy and kept their money, but didn't actually say that zakat is not obligatory, he viewed them as rebels against the state, but still within the fold of Islam.

So the point being that on this issue of whether they're within or outside of Islam, the sahaba themselves showed us we need to have an understanding of what is a Muslim and what isn't a Muslim. As well, the first splinter group to break away from orthodoxy broke away over this issue. And this is of course the Kharijites, or the Khawarij. And it's very, very interesting to note that this issue of defining who is a Muslim was the first issue that the Ummah was obsessed over, and that one faction broke away because of. It's a very important issue.

Also, very important to point out that this issue is very, very dangerous. And we see this from the very beginning of Islam. That is why to err on the side of caution is better. Because we see what happens historically when groups take this issue to be the most important. The Kharijites went fanatical in this regard, and they deemed everybody who disagreed with them to be kafir. And their fanaticism caused many other Muslims to go to the other extreme, which is to say, let's not even talk about this issue. But we don't fight extremism with another extremism. We fight extremism with the middle path. We fight extremism with wisdom and knowledge.

Just because one group of fanatics went berserk (and they did go berserk; they started excommunicating the rest of the Muslim world, they started killing people, and we have these groups up until our times, these fanatical groups that are going to bomb other masajid or kill other people in the name of Islam, thinking that their other Muslim brothers are kafir), that doesn't change the fact that sometimes a belief might be wrong or a belief might be kufr. But we're not saying we should be violent against them. The fact that some fanatics were violent does not change the reality of what is right and wrong. We correct the violence, we speak out against the violence, and we preach with wisdom and we preach tolerance.

This is the fine line here. It's very difficult to do, I understand, but that is what our religion requires us to do. We preach a version of tolerance, not necessarily the full Western version of "I'm okay, you're okay." We don't believe that. We are not all the same when it comes to beliefs. There are beliefs that are orthodox and mainstream and beloved to Allah and His Messenger, and there are beliefs that are wrong. We preach the correct belief. We say this is the right belief. And then we categorize other beliefs as being wrong, as being deviant, as being within Islam but not upon orthodoxy, or as being outside the fold of Islam.

And along with all of this, we always preach tolerance of humanity, tolerance of live and let live. We are not forcing anyone. It is always, unequivocally, no exceptions, haram to force a person to accept your belief by threat of sword or death or killing. This is unequivocally haram; we do not impose our beliefs on other people. The fact that we do not impose our beliefs on other people does not change the fact that we might disagree with their beliefs.

So that is one of the points that I need to stress: that the issue of who is and isn't a Muslim has been something that our Ummah has been occupied with since the beginning of our tradition. And there have been extremist movements, and there continue to be extremist movements, in this regard. And in fact, every single firqah, every single theology since the beginning of Islam, one of the things that it discusses is what is correct theology, and then what is incorrect theology but still Islam, and then what is incorrect theology outside of Islam.

So for our purposes, let's just say there are two simple boundaries, right? Even though, of course, there's much more than this, for our purposes let's say there are two milestones. The first milestone is when you're outside of orthodoxy but still a Muslim. So your theology is wrong, but not to the level of being non-Muslim, okay? This is what is called Ahlul Bid'ah, or the people of deviation. That level is one level. Then you have another level outside, which is the theology that negates your Islam: you're outside the fold of Islam. Every single group since the beginning of Islam has discussed these two areas and has attempted to codify what it believes is correct in this regard, and you will find variations within all of the movements and groups. Now, I'm not going to go into all of that controversy, but realize that this is a topic of controversy within the various groups.

My opinion about this (and this is an area of my expertise, the theology), my opinion about this is very clear. The position I advocate is very clear, and that is that to be a Muslim, to go from non-Muslim to Muslim, to leave kufr and to enter Islam, what is required is very simple. And that is the Kalima and all that is necessitated by the Kalima. That's it. La ilaha illa Allah, Muhammadur Rasulullah, and what this Kalima entails. If you do this and you follow this up without bringing something that negates the Kalima, then you are within the fold of Islam.

So anyone who believes that Allah is their Lord and Creator and object of worship, anyone who wants to worship Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and takes Muhammad ﷺ as the Messenger of Allah, the one whom we turn to for how we worship Allah, for our guidance, for our role model, that person is within the fold of Islam, as long as nothing comes that negates that simple Kalima of La ilaha illallah Muhammadur Rasulullah, and anything that is obviously necessitated by that. Anybody who believes in something that negates the Kalima is not a Muslim anymore. It's that simple.

And again, you need to understand this point. If somebody were to worship an idol and say this idol created me, and to sacrifice to the idol, how can we say this is Islam? It is not Islam, right? Similarly, if somebody says there is a Nabi after our Nabi ﷺ that we turn to for guidance, right, there is a human being after our Prophet ﷺ that Allah inspired, there is simply no question that this is outside the fold of Islam, because the Kalima necessitates this: the seal of the prophets, that our Prophet ﷺ is the final messenger. And in fact the companions did not differ over the fact that Musaylama and all of these false prophets that came are outside the fold of Islam, unequivocally, without any controversy. There is no excuse for a person who believes in a prophet after the Prophet ﷺ. So that is how we defined kufr and Islam.

Now, within Islam, what is the overall orthodoxy, or what we call Sunni, or Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah? My position is that anybody who takes the Qur'an and the Sunnah as their primary sources, and they affirm what is in the famous Hadith of Jibreel, which is the five pillars of Islam (the actions are there) and the six pillars of iman, if they affirm this, then generally speaking they are within mainstream orthodoxy. And the differences beyond this are too petty to make a major issue.

You know, within mainstream Sunnism there are lots and lots of variations and interpretations. And whether it is Deobandi, or whether it is Tablighi, whether it is Barelvi, whether it is Ahl-e-Hadith and Salafi, all of these, generally speaking, should discuss amongst themselves with an element of civility and an element of brotherhood. That is different than if we are discussing with somebody who is outside of all of this. So what they have in common is a lot more than what others have, and there should not be any level of extreme animosity or hostility. Not that there should be with other groups as well, but I'm saying especially when it comes to those who affirm the Qur'an and Sunnah, and those who respect the companions, and those who believe in the six pillars of iman as in the Hadith of Jibreel. In this case they are, generally speaking, upon a very similar understanding of Islam.

Now obviously somebody who rejects one of these six pillars of iman, doesn't believe in Qadr, somebody who rejects the companions, doesn't accept the books of hadith or whatnot, obviously they're now heading into territory that is not orthodox. And this is a different interpretation of Islam. And, you know, that doesn't mean we are uncivil to them, but no doubt there's a level of difference now where it's not the same, and we understand that this is an incorrect belief system, even as we live with them in civil society.

Now, another point here that's very, very important, and unfortunately many even preachers and scholars fall into this mistake, is that they don't differentiate between speaking in generalities and applying specifics. What do I mean by this? We are obliged by Allah to speak in generalities. We are not obliged by Allah to pronounce verdicts on people, especially when we're not qualified to do so. Pronouncing verdicts on individuals is not the same as speaking in generalities. We as preachers and teachers must teach the masses. You as parents must teach your children generalities. Do not teach them, in fact warn them against, specifics.

What do I mean by this? Let me give you an example. We teach our children that we dislike kufr and shirk. We teach our children that it is wrong to worship other than Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. We teach our children that we do not make fun of Islam or anything of Islam. We teach our children that to make fun of Islam, to make fun of the Qur'an, to make fun of Allah and His Messenger, this is kufr. We teach our children that to curse the companions is heresy and deviation; we should not do this. So we teach them the general rules.

Okay, now we come across somebody, in some YouTube video, whatever, who is a Muslim, he thinks he's a Muslim, and he cracks a joke that seems to make fun of Islam. Okay, we have just taught our children that making fun of anything of Islam is kufr, which it is. You don't make fun of Allah and His Messenger. You don't make fun of something that Allah commands you to do. So we find somebody that we think is doing this. Do we then say, "Oh, this person is a kafir"? Even though we have just said that making fun of Allah is kufr, making fun of the Prophet is kufr, now we find somebody doing it: do we automatically translate the rule, which is that making fun of Islam is kufr, into a specific verdict, which is "You are a kafir"?

The answer to this: **the lay person is not allowed to take a general rule and apply it to a specific person.** That is something that is a fatwa that is done by the people of ifta, the people of knowledge. You (when I say you, I mean, of course, the general lay Muslim, the average Muslim) are not obliged. In fact, it is dangerous to open this door of stamping people and applying generalities to specifics. So if you find somebody who is actually making fun of something Islamic, you may ask a Shaykh or an 'Alim, or the Mufti may look into this issue, but as a person who is not trained, you do not pronounce a verdict on the person. You may pronounce it on the action: "Hey, this is wrong, you should not be doing this."

Why? Because to translate a principle into a reality, to translate a general rule from a textbook into a lived reality, this requires knowledge that the textbook will not give you. And the Shaykh or the 'Alim or the Mufti has to look at many things. First and foremost, for example, you yourself might be mistaken. You might think it's kufr, but it's not kufr. You interpreted it to be kufr, but it is not kufr; your own knowledge misunderstood whether it is kufr or not. And we see this all the time: so often somebody says something that the other person interprets as, "Oh, that is making fun of Allah and His Messenger," but he is simply making a statement of fact.

And an example can be if a Christian, an actual Christian, says, "I don't believe in your prophet," for example, right? That is his belief. Of course he doesn't believe in our Prophet. In an Islamic land, in an ideal Islamic land, this is not blasphemy for him to say, "I believe in Jesus, the Son of God, and I don't believe in your Prophet." That is the definition of being Christian. In some Muslim lands, if a Christian says this, the people, the villagers, go berserk on him: "This is blasphemy, this is gustakh-e-rasul," and this and that. No, it's not. He is simply telling you, or she is simply telling you, what she believes as a Christian. That is the definition of Christianity. If she believed, or if he believed, that the Prophet ﷺ is a prophet, then they wouldn't be a Christian, would they? So you understood this to be derogatory, but it is not derogatory. And therefore, again, you misapplied a general rule, and you didn't understand what that general rule is.

Another principle is: the person who commits this action, is he or she even aware that it is wrong? Do they even know? Do they understand the severity? Do they understand that this is something that Allah has forbidden? Maybe they don't know any better. And ignorance is an excuse in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. You can be excused if you don't know.

And the famous example of this is the man our Prophet ﷺ mentioned, that he had committed some bad deeds and he was worried that Allah might punish him. So what did he do? He told his children, when I die, cremate my body and scatter the ashes everywhere, so that Allah cannot resurrect me, right? Because he said, if Allah resurrects me, then He's going to punish me, and I don't want to be punished. Now, he thought that his action could outwit Allah. He thought that separating his body into ashes was going to allow him to be scot-free. In other words, he thought he is more powerful than Allah, but he didn't actually think that. It's his innocence; it's his simple mind. And our Prophet ﷺ said Allah commanded the winds to gather his ashes, resurrected him, and said to the man, "Why did you do this?" And the man said, "I was scared of You, O Allah." And so Allah forgave him because of his innocence, that "I was scared of You," not because of the deed.

Here, if you were to ask me, what is the verdict of a person who thinks he can outwit Allah, and who thinks he can do something so that he's not going to be resurrected? I will say, and any scholar will say, that is kufr; that is major kufr. No one is more powerful than Allah, and it is kufr. But the man was so ignorant, we can say he was such a simpleton, that in his understanding he was doing it out of innocence, and Allah forgave him because of that, right? So again, we speak in generics. We do not apply specifics until many conditions have been met.

Also, we can say: what if there was a mistake? What if there was an emotional issue, that he just became overwhelmed? What if he lost his mind temporarily and did something he shouldn't have done? And we find this in the hadith of Bukhari and Muslim, a very long example, of a man who became delirious out of happiness. He thought he was about to die; he discovers he's not going to die, and he shouts out out of joy, "Oh, I am Allah's Lord, and Allah is my servant," a'udhu billah. That's what he says. And our Prophet ﷺ excused him and said he was so happy that he made a mistake. He was so happy that he blurted it out; he didn't mean to say that. So even our Prophet ﷺ excused this phrase, and that's because his emotions got the better of him.

And of course, there are always other issues: was he forced, this and that? My point being that we need to be very careful about speaking in generalities versus speaking in specifics. And unfortunately, many of our preachers don't make this point clear, and they teach in a manner such that they expect you to take those generalities and apply them in specifics. I advise the preachers (and I hope I'm doing this all the time) that we keep on distinguishing between speaking in general tones versus applying that tone to a specific person. There is no question that this issue is abused and misused.

Now, once we understand this, what should a society do, an Islamic society, about people who have different beliefs? How should they be treated? This is where I say that the shari'ah does have a spectrum of differences that can be done. Theoretically, it doesn't matter where you are in the world: something that is wrong is something that is wrong. A deviant belief is a deviant belief. Theoretically, it doesn't matter; an action is kufr or shirk wherever you are, or it's not kufr or shirk. However, realistically, there are certain things that will change the application. There are certain things that are mitigating factors that change from society to culture to time to place.

And therefore, how these other groups should be treated is a culture-specific and a time-specific and a place-specific question. In Baghdad of the third century of the Hijrah, for example, maybe we can say our scholars treated these other groups very harshly, and they had every right to do so. It was a different world, different time, different place. Should we treat somebody in modern-day Pakistan or in modern-day America or modern-day other lands the same way? It depends on the culture and the time and the place and the scholars of every region: the fair-minded, open-minded, forward-thinking scholars. And again, who you choose is up to you in this regard. So you're going to find scholars of the entire spectrum here. But that is something that is culture-specific.

And I have said this many, many times: to take the position of how heretic groups were treated in Mamluk times or in Abbasid times or in Umayyad times, and to apply them in America or even in Pakistan, is very, very incorrect. Times have changed and situations have changed. And what might have been major deviancy back in the 3rd century of the Hijrah, in light of what we are facing now becomes minor deviancy. We have bigger challenges, different challenges. Our children are leaving Islam. So these sectarian issues automatically become far more trivial. Differences in interpretation are not how they used to be in the past. The freedoms that our societies give are also things that we're going to have to take into account.

And therefore, without mentioning names of these groups: our sister mentions two names. The first is the majority non-Sunni group. By the way, I'm not mentioning names for this particular question. I have mentioned these names in other lectures, but for this question I want to keep it theoretical. I have spoken about these other groups in other lectures; I don't need to mention them specifically here. But our sister says that, for example, there's a group that is non-Sunni, and they're always being cursed and maligned, and they curse us back, and this and that.

And my position has always been that, look, this group that does not respect the Sahaba, that believes in a series of Imams and whatnot, definitely they are not mainstream orthodox Muslims. They have beliefs that are problematic; there's no question about that. At the same time, generally speaking, they are definitely within the fold of Islam. They believe in the Kalima, they believe in Allah, they face the qibla, they do wudu, they fast Ramadan, they read the Qur'an. The sha'a'ir, or the main teachings of Islam, are found amongst them. And this is the essence of what it means to be non-mainstream, or what is called Ahlul Bid'ah. This is exactly what it is. They are Muslims, but they are not within what we consider to be orthodoxy. Allah will be their judge.

Also realize the vast majority of all of these non-Sunni groups are simply following what their parents taught them. And if they are innocent, and they are sincere, and they are pious in their own way, inshallah they will be forgiven by Allah, because they don't know any better. Let me ask you an honest question: aren't you a Sunni because your parents are Sunnis? For the majority of us, that is the case. We are taught a version of Islam, and we accept that version of Islam. Now, I have gone on a study, and I have studied intensely; I believe that what I believe is authentic. But that's my belief at the end of the day.

The other innocent Muslim out there, who is born in another firqah, another group, another sect, is taught another paradigm, another perspective. And they firmly believe that that is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught them. They firmly believe that the Ahl al-Bayt have a status, and Fatima is this and Ali is that and Hussain is this. Okay, that is their belief. I disagree with it. And I will politely preach and teach a different version of Islam. And I will never preach hatred of another group or individual. But I will say that it is incorrect to believe that there are Imams that are doing things and are still alive, or this. We're going to say this is incorrect belief, and it's not supported by the Qur'an or by the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.

Nonetheless, we will allow them to be who they are. In fact, we will respect their humanity without respecting their beliefs. This is a very key point here, right? I will not respect the beliefs of those who are saying bad things about the Sahaba, but I can give them the right to be who they are. I don't have to force my beliefs on them. They are who they are. I don't like it, but I'm not going to preach civil war. I'm not going to preach that they should be harmed. I'm going to preach tolerance. I'm going to preach that, okay, we have to agree to disagree; I don't agree with what you are saying. And this is in fact exactly what Ali radiyallahu 'anhu himself did when it came to the Kharijites: he allowed them to be who they are without forcing Sunnism onto them. So we have to agree to disagree.

Now, what if they believe something that is outside the fold of Islam? In this case, we say that ignorance is not an excuse. Ignorance might be an excuse if you're within Islam: if you believe in Imams, you believe in this and that, you know, ignorance is an excuse; you believe in the Kalima. But if you believe that other than Allah is your Lord and you claim to be Muslim, there is no excuse. And if you believe in a Nabi after our Nabi ﷺ, there is no excuse. Everybody should know that the message of the Qur'an is very clear, and everyone in that group who believes otherwise cannot be considered a Muslim.

Now, that does not mean that we harm them, we execute them, we throw them in jail, we persecute them. It simply is a point that we don't believe they are Muslim. And whether they should live in a particular land or not is something that is up to the government. And I don't see any problem whatsoever if we treat this group like we treat other non-Muslim groups. In that land that you mentioned, there are people who worship idols, and that is the worst sin in our religion, to worship an idol. But they are citizens of the land, and they have the right to do what they are doing. They are not considered Muslim. They have their religion.

> لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِيَ دِينِ

So we should also understand that it is not a problem Islamically to allow these groups to practice their version of their faith and to do what they are doing. And we have the right to say that that is wrong and that is not within the fold of Islam. They have the right to not be harmed and to go about their daily lives within a fully Islamic land. Obviously, in a land where religion does not play a role in society, where the government is totally neutral and all religions are free, even more so they have the right to do as they please, because we too have the right to do as we please.

The bottom line with this, inshallah (we move on to the other question; I hope I've answered some of your points): it is very important to discuss correct beliefs from incorrect beliefs, but that does not translate into treating people nicely versus treating people badly. **We can say this belief is wrong and still treat somebody cordially.** This is what we need to get across. Anyone who says that this idol created me, I think this is the worst thing you can say theologically. Still, if I were to meet this person, I will smile, I will be nice and polite. My assessment of his belief does not translate into me treating that person rudely. That's what we need to understand here.

And so the same applies to these other movements, these other firqas, these other groups as well. We preach correct theology. We advise our children, our community, to what is correct theology. We try to correct incorrect theology in a wise manner. But we do not preach hatred. We do not preach firqabazi, as you call it in Urdu. We do not preach violence. We do not preach forcing other people to adopt any other belief system.

> لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِيَ دِينِ

And that is the middle line that we need to try to find. And we ask Allah 'azza wa jal to help us in this regard.
